content: systems might be attributed to the fact that their tempers and natural inclinations exposed them to the temptation and allurement of preferring intellectual speculation to the practice of their faith. Both were, after all, habitually bookish men, of a scholarly cast of mind, possessed of rare dialectical skill and tenaciously logical. Yet their dis- t~st is more deeply founded than this. It derives from the mere Christian's distinction between the few essential dog- mas and the many (and varied) systems men have built upon them. When platforms and doctrines have been relegated to a subordinate position there remains only the practice of the essentials as the sure mark of the true Christian: "the holy practical Christian is the best and only true Christian" Baxter wrote. 39 To expend time and energy upon doctrinal speculation is hence to misdirect the effort which should properly be devoted to Christian works. A consequence of the mere Christian's readiness to admit the legitimacy (and hence the indifference) of any number of theological schemes is thus the insistence that practice alone is the Christian's real business. As a writer the mere Christian is hence a casuist and a moralist rather than a systematic theologian. It is no accident that Lewis' best known book, The Screwtape Letters, is remarkable amongst modern works of moral divinity for its detailed attention to the workaday, humdrum and menial business of everyday temptations. It is similarly with the experience of everyman that Baxter's semi-fictional The Poor Man's Family Book (1674) is, like all his practical writings, concerned. It follows that controversial divinity gets short shrift from the mere Christian. Baxter consistently advised his readers against exposing themselves to the unsettling and unedifying effects of controversy: "You may believe there is a God, long before you arc fit to hear an Atheist proving that there is no God. ,,40 And although Lewis is certainly disputatious he is so on behalf of mere Christianity against the arguments of atheism, agnosticism and moral relativism. He rarely engaged in controversy upon specific theological points within the Christian tradition, and never debates them for their own sake. He is led into controversial areas only when they impinge upon practice: he takes up our con- ception of God the Father and the significance of Christ's masculinity, for example, only because of their bearing upon human sexual relationships.4l It is the application of doc- trine which is primary. Similarly, it was the dire practical consequences of antinomianism which led Baxter to exempt this from his general embargo on partisan controversy and to com- bat it throughout his life, from his first publication, Aphorismes of Justification (1649), until one of his last, The Scripture Gospel Defended (1690). And since it is in the spiritual life (and not in theological, ecclesiastical or liturgical traditions) that catholic Christianity consists, the mere Christian prizes the inner, meditative life, giving us Baxter's Saints Rest and Lewis' Reflections on the Psalms and Letters to Malcolm, Chiefly on Prayer. Baxter's own intellectual development consisted in large part of shedding his early scholarly delight in doctrine for its own sake. In his youth he was desirous of "Literate Fame," "the highest Academical Degrees and Reputation of Learning" and was soon "running up into a multitude of Con- troversies, and greatly delighted with metaphysical and scholastick Writings." However, "the elder I grew the smal- ler stress I layd upon these Controversies and curiosities" until "now it is the fundamental Doctrines of the Catechism, which I highliest value.,,42 It was to the exposition and application of these fundamentals that he devoted those of his books he most prized, for It was never the will of God that bare speculation should be the end of his Revelation, or of our be- lief. Divinity is an Affective practical Science . . . . effectual apprehensions of the Riches of Grace and the Glory to come, and yet never heard of most the Questions in Scotus, or Ockham or Aquinas's sums, is far richer in knowledge, and a much wiser man than he that hath these Controversies at his fingers ends. 44 A facility in theological discussion is therefore no guide to a man's spiritual state: he "that hath spent ten or twenty or thirty years in studies" and is "pufft up because he can speak more congruously than an honest plowman" and is prone to despise "honest vulgar Christians" and "ordinary men that could never speak or write true English" is a fool and a hypocrite. 4 5 We are reminded of the contempt felt by the rationalist Greek, the FOx, for common, unlearned people in Till We Have Faces, and that this representative of intel- lectual culture comes to learn that all his wisdom is mere glibness, that his "prattle of maxims" is further from the truth than the ignorant superstitions of barbarians. 46 Lewis is here turning his back upon his own erudition quite as firmly as Baxter had done. We meet just this bias in Narnia. The chronicles are much concerned with action: debate, when it occurs, is generally debate as to what, in any predicament, it is best to do. It is true that adventure is good material for chil- dren's stories (and certainly better than abstract theologi- cal discussion!) but this is not the whole truth. Asian's concern for behavior and performance (the children are always called into Narnia to perform a task) reflects the inevitable stress of the mere Christian. The inarticulate Cabby--Baxter's "honest plowman" to the life--in The Magician's Nephew, the unbeliever Trumpkin in Prince Caspian, the pessimistic Puddle- glum in The Silver Chair and the Calormene Emeth in The Last Battle all demonstrate Lewis' willingness to follow Baxter in judging of them by their love rather than by their opinions, intellectual attitudes or religious allegiance. In Lewis' non-fictional work Baxter's conviction reappears in the same words: "Theology is practical." The invidious attraction of a vague theism or pantheism was, for Lewis, precisely that "It is all thrills and no work. ,,47 Essay I 38 by guest on July 26, 2015 cal.sagepub.com

If the attention of the mere Christian is firmly focused on the business in hand then he will neglect not only theo- logical fashions and debates but also himself. Baxter shared the Puritan preoccupation with self-scrutiny, but this was not a preoccupation with self: it was an exercise in the judicial assessment of the self's performance, a "casting up of accounts" as it was often called. Baxter's famous self- review in the Reliquiae Baxterianae (1696) is an account of how his opinions have changed, a history of development, and not a characterization of himself or a record of the details of his private life. Indeed, he begins the self-re- view by dissociating himself from an untoward curiosity about men's inner experiences and personalities: "And for any more particular Account of Heart-Occurrences, and God's Operations on me, I think it somewhat unsavory to recite them; seeing God's Dealings are much what the same with all his Servants in the main.,,48 We meet something very like that "unsavory" at the beginning of Lewis' i1.utobiographical Surprised by Joy: "From my earliest years I was aware of the vivid contrast between my mother's cheerful and tranquil affection and the ups and downs of my father's emotional life, and this bred in me long before I was old enough to give it a name a certain distrust or dislike of emotion.,,49 And Lewis never would reveal the emotional details of his inner life, not even in that apparently most subjective of books, A Grief Observed. Surprised by Joy itself is (as Lewis himself re- marked in its preface) reticent and selective, not an auto- biography proper but, like the earlier allegorical version, The Pilgrim's Regress, the history of a conversion. As such, it belongs to a venerable tradition, but that Lewis should have preferred this genre to a full autobiography is indica- tive of his bias. His neglect of himself was something far more deep-rooted than the neglect of his clothes and appear- ance to which photographs testify, and something rather teasing and ambivalent. It perplexed and puzzled his close friend Owen Barfield who, more than once, suspected Lewis was posturing, not being himself but assuming roles. certainly true that Lewis' early poetry has much of pastiche in it; that there is an element of performance, a deliberate- ly assumed persona, in his vigorously argued and belligerent- ly manly apologetics; and that burlesque, caricature and parody remain staple techniques of his fiction. If such techniques raise doubts about the maturity of Lewis' grasp of human character, his life-long guerrilla campaign against psychology, which at times assumed the proportions of an ob- session, can suggest a fraught anxiety to safeguard the secrets of his own self. On the other hand, any further characterization of the hero of The Screwtape Letters would have detracted from its incisive depiction of moral struggle, and just how positive this aspect of Lewis could be is evi- denced by his masterpiece, Till We Have Faces, where the shedding of inhibiting personality is the way to the freedom of faith. Whichever view one takes, OWen Barfield has neat- ly pointed to the similarity of emphasis with Baxter in his comment that Lewis "at a certain stage in his life . deliberately ceased to take any interest in himself except as a kind of spiritual alumnus taking his moral finals."SO There is the concern for performance. It would, however, be unjust to give the impression that for the mere Christian his faith is all work and no play. Play, even Bacchanalian play at the end of Prince Caspian, figures large in Narnia, and there is the striking climax to That Hideous Strength, "Venus over St. Anne's," to remind us that joy, and joy involving all the senses of man, is a legit- imate pleasure and true blessing in Lewis' thought. And for Baxter, too, "there is sweetness in the work and way of God ... the life of Christianity is a life of Joy"Sl which leads, 52 in the phrase both men use, to an eternal weight of glory. There are those who feel Lewis' work fails because it so resolutely sets its face against the twentieth century. The historian Christopher Hill is by no means alone in seeing Lewis as "old fashioned" and so out of court. will but supply further proof of his irrelevance. Has not the world moved on since the time of Cromwell? Perhaps it has. Lewis' responsiveness to Baxter's insight, however, proves him not so much old-fashioned as immune to the fashions of any age. The renewed life given to Baxter's phrase three centuries later is a salutary reminder that while the world may indeed "progress" through intellectual fads and fashions, catholic Christianity is what it always was, "quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est.,,54 NOTES 1. .
